data.title: Wall Street ends higher as battered AI stocks gain in volatile week
data.description:
NEW YORK - Wall Street’s main indexes ended higher on Nov 27 and posted weekly gains as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday and flocked to hard-hit AI-linked shares.

US stocks have swung sharply this week, with Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO and Anthropic’s brief fall below its initial public offering price adding to volatility across the AI trade.

Investors have alternated between bargain-hunting after a steep selloff and fretting over soaring AI costs, heavy borrowing and doubts about companies’ returns on investment.

“The market is so oversold that a bounce was inevitable,” said Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group.

Chipmakers that investors battered this month recovered ground, with Micron and Marvell gaining 7.6% and 7.3% respectively. The broader chip gauge also climbed 4.7%. Nvidia, after remaining weak for most of the session, ended 0.8% higher.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94, the S&P 500 gained 114.71 points, or 1.60%, to 7,297.49 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 543.70 points, or 2.31%, to 24,129.50.

AI beneficiaries, including data-storage firm Sandisk , surged almost 16%, while optical-products maker Lumentum and server maker Dell also gained sharply.

AI hyperscalers – tech companies that run large data centers – also rose, with Amazon.com, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle posting gains. Tesla surged 5%.

“There is a bounce in technology which started Monday, continued Wednesday with an intraday reversal and now continues today. So much fast money has delevered out of tech that this could have persistence next week as they are forced to chase back in,” said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Weekly gains

For the week, the S&P 500 gained 5.6%, the Nasdaq rose 6.68%, and the Dow climbed 5.46%. The S&P 500 weekly gain was the index’s biggest since April 2025.

The S&P 500 bank index rose 1.6%, fuelled by JPMorgan Chase’s almost 2% gain.

The market’s gains have done little to erase November’s losses. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq are on track for their worst November since 2008, pressured by concerns over tougher AI regulation following the Democrats’ US midterm election victory and expectations that monetary policy will remain restrictive.

Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December after data this week showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated further in October.

Gold and silver miners rallied as precious-metal prices recovered from a bruising few sessions. Newmont gained 5.4%, while the Global X Silver Miners ETF also advanced.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals slid 5.2% after the US Food and Drug Administration extended its review of the company’s kidney-disease drug by up to three months.

US equity markets were open for a half-day session on Nov 27, following the Thanksgiving holiday on Nov 26.

Volume on US exchanges was 10.97 billion shares.

Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.25-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 55 new highs and 73 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 3,677 stocks rose and 1,135 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.24-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 96 new lows. REUTERS

data.title: Airline Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
data.description:
OSLO – Budget carrier Norse Atlantic said on Nov 27 it would file a petition for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit and was halting ticket sales and cancelling all flights, becoming the latest airline casualty of fuel-cost spikes stemming from the war in Iran.

Norse is the second European airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings in 2026 after Latvia’s airBaltic, highlighting the toll of the Iran war on carriers that entered the crisis without fuel hedges as jet fuel prices surged.

The company said it had not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs, with the board deciding to file a bankruptcy petition on Nov 27 with the Agder District Court in Norway for its operating subsidiary.

“The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations,” Norse’s chief executive officer Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Roald held a virtual meeting with Norse’s employees at 1pm GMT, according to Norwegian media.

The company had 1,071 employees as at June 30, its latest quarterly filing showed.

The airline is advising passengers against going to the airport as it has stopped flying, adding that customers could submit a claim for a refund in the insolvency process, though that would not guarantee payment, while customer service is no longer available.

“This is a very hard day for the pilots and their families, and for all other Norse employees. Our thoughts are also with the passengers whose journeys are now cancelled,” the board of the Norse Atlantic Pilots Association told Reuters in a statement.

Aircraft owners terminate leases

Norse Atlantic said on Nov 25 that its financial situation was “critical”. The following day, it said it had suspended all flights and that the board could file for bankruptcy unless it urgently secured funding.

Earlier on Nov 27, Norse said its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier’s fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back, a claim contested by the company.

Norse in 2021 signed long-term leases for nine Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft from Ireland-based AerCap Holdings and six Dreamliners from Singapore-based BOC Aviation. It later returned three of the planes to AerCap.

“The company contests the validity of the termination notices,” Norse said in a statement.

The AerCap leases were due to run for about 12 years for each aircraft, while the BOC contracts were due to run for 16 years, according to Norse’s latest annual report.

“Although they are contesting the notices, it sounds pretty decisive. Unless successful in this, they will not be able to resume operations,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.

BOC declined to comment when contacted by Reuters. AerCap did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Worst aviation crisis since pandemic

Founded in 2021 by entrepreneur Bjorn Tore Larsen, Norse sought to revive budget transatlantic flights after Norwegian Air abandoned long-haul operations during the pandemic.

But as a pure long-haul player, Norse Atlantic lacked a “feeder” service from regional connections, which industry analysts early on said could hamper efforts to fill the start-up carrier’s transatlantic flights.

The airline later diversified into charter and aircraft leasing services as it struggled to generate profits from scheduled flights alone.

The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the Covid-19 pandemic as the US-Iran conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines’ costs skyrocketing. REUTERS

data.title: Sri Lanka credit rating upgraded
data.description:
COLOMBO – An international agency upgraded Sri Lanka’s credit rating to B- on Nov 27, its first change in more than a year, as the island nation continues its economic recovery.

S&P Global Ratings said it reflected efforts to strengthen fiscal and external buffers since the 2022 crisis, when the country defaulted on US$46 billion (S$59.31 billion) in external debt.

It raised Sri Lanka’s foreign currency and local currency sovereign credit ratings from CCC+ to B-, with a stable outlook.

In September 2025, S&P removed Sri Lanka from “Selective Default” status, assigning it a junk rating of CCC+.

Sri Lanka secured a US$2.9 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout after the crisis, which is expected to be fully disbursed by March.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake unveiled his 2027 budget in November, projecting US$2.08 billion in foreign funding.

The IMF forecasts that Sri Lanka’s growth will slow to 4% in 2026 from 5% in 2025, as higher global energy costs weigh on the economy.

It has said Sri Lanka has proved “remarkably resilient to successive shocks” but has also warned of risks from the Middle East war, global trade uncertainty and the El Nino climate phenomenon. AFP

data.title: Real incomes in S’pore rise but at slower pace in 2026, with smaller gains for lower-wage workers
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Workers in Singapore saw their incomes grow in 2026 but at a slower pace, after taking higher inflation into account.

Real median income of full-time employed residents rose by 2.2% in 2026, down from 4.1% in 2025.

For workers at the 20th percentile of the income distribution, real income growth slowed to 1.3%, from 3.6% the year before.

The nominal median monthly income of full-time resident workers – before accounting for inflation – rose to $6,021 in 2026, up from $5,775 in 2025. This is the first time the figure has exceeded $6,000. For 20th-percentile earners, it grew by 3.4% to $3,270, from $3,164 in 2025.

The figures were released by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) on Nov 27 in its annual labour force advance report.

The figures are preliminary as full-year inflation data for 2026 is not yet available.

MOM said the slower growth partly reflected more cautious wage increases by firms and higher inflation. Consumer prices are projected to rise by around 2% in 2026, compared with 0.9% in 2025.

The ministry said that despite the slower gains for lower-wage workers in 2026, their incomes have grown faster than those at the median over the recent five- and 10-year periods.

It added that they will continue to be supported by progressive wage measures.

Permanent jobs remain the norm

MOM noted that employment quality remained broadly stable even with softening manpower demand and continued external uncertainty.

Employees accounted for 88.2% of employed residents in 2026.

Among resident employees, 91% held permanent jobs, edging up from 90.8% in 2025.

The share of employees on fixed-term contracts remained stable at 7.1%, while casual or on-call employment declined further to 2%.

Over the decade, there was a shift among fixed-term contract employees towards longer contracts of at least a year, the ministry said.

Unemployment rates

While Singapore’s unemployment rate stayed low overall, there were signs of greater pressure on workers in non-professional roles.

The unemployment rate among non-professionals, managers, executives and technicians (non-PMETs) rose from 2.8% in 2025 to 3.5% in 2026, returning to levels seen in 2023 and 2024.

In contrast, unemployment among PMETs remained broadly stable at 2.7%.

The long-term unemployment rate, which measures the proportion of workers who have been unemployed for at least 25 weeks, edged up to 0.7% for both groups.

Among non-PMETs, the increase was driven by workers aged 50 and above.

Residents in their 50s recorded the highest incidence of retrenchment, rising from 2.4 to 3.6 per 1,000 employees between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026.

Their six-month re-entry rate was also consistently below the overall average.

MOM said at a briefing on Nov 27 that the increase in the unemployment rate for non-PMETs can be attributed to difficulties faced by older non-PMETs in securing employment.

The hiring conditions in certain sectors also softened. The long-term unemployment rate in sectors more exposed to the global economy, such as manufacturing and wholesale trade, rose from 0.7% in 2025 to a five-year high of 0.9% in 2026.

Overqualification

With the Singapore workforce being increasingly educated, the share of resident workers in PMET jobs rose to 65.2%.

But the overqualification rate has declined for the third consecutive year from 19.4% in 2025 to 18.7% in 2026, while the involuntary overqualification rate remained low at 1.6%. The latter suggests that a few workers were in jobs below their qualifications because they could not find suitable alternatives, MOM said.

The profiles of the voluntarily and involuntarily overqualified were “broadly similar”. Of the tertiary-educated, 47.7% worked as associate professionals, while 50.8% worked as technicians. This reflects younger workers taking up entry-level jobs to gain experience for higher-skilled jobs, MOM said.

Labour under-utilisation, which refers to the unemployed, under-employed and discouraged workers, remained low in 2026.

The number of discouraged workers, which refers to people who gave up on their job search, remained low at 7,100, or 0.3% of the resident labour force.

There has been a slight dip in the proportion of part-time workers who are willing and available to do additional work, with the time-related under-employment rate declining from 1.9% in 2025 to 1.7% in 2026.

Ageing workforce

Singapore’s labour force participation rate eased further for the fifth consecutive year since 2021, but remains largely stable despite its ageing population, hovering at 67.9% in 2025 and 67.8% in 2026.

Higher participation among women has helped to offset some of the pressures of an ageing population.

The labour force participation rate rose across most five-year age groups, with larger increases among seniors.

Coupled with seniors’ growing share in the population, the proportion of residents aged 60 years and above in the labour force rose from 13.1% in 2016 to 19.5% in 2026.

Singapore’s labour force participation rate also ranked among the world’s highest – placing seventh across the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s member countries – ahead of countries such as Switzerland, Estonia and Australia, MOM noted.

The findings in the advance labour force report were drawn from the annual Comprehensive Labour Force Survey, which covers a representative sample of 33,000 households. A total of 27,292 households responded to the survey conducted from March to July.

data.title: Fewer people in S’pore changed jobs in 2026, but most who did earned more: MOM
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Fewer workers in Singapore have been changing jobs as hiring slows and more seek job stability, even though those who have switched employers have been more likely to get a higher pay.

About two-thirds, or 65.6%, of full-time resident employees aged 25 to 64 who changed jobs saw their incomes rise after accounting for inflation, with most of these gains amounting to at least 5%.

The figures were released by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) on Nov 27 in its annual labour force advance report.

The proportion of employed residents who changed jobs in the past year fell to 5.7% in 2026, extending the gradual downtrend from its peak in 2022.

The decline in job switching was most pronounced among younger residents aged below 30, particularly those aged 15 to 24. Younger workers who stayed in their jobs cited job stability as the most common reason for staying.

Meanwhile, older workers aged 50 and above were least likely to change jobs, with around half of older job stayers holding on to their current jobs for at least a decade.

MOM also tracked the longer-term income outcomes of workers who changed jobs, and found that they were more likely to enjoy real income gains than those who did not, director of MOM’s manpower research and statistics department Ang Boon Heng noted at a media briefing on Nov 27.

Job switchers were more likely than job stayers to see real income gains, with about 67% of them receiving higher incomes from 2025 to 2026, compared with around 61% who stayed in their jobs.

The gap widens when looking at a five-year period from 2021 to 2026. For example, the older cohort who changed jobs in 2021 saw their incomes rise over a longer period following the job switch.

More than nine in 10 job switches over the past year were voluntary rather than due to retrenchments, said MOM.

Income outcomes were weaker in a small segment of workers who changed jobs involuntarily. Around 58% enjoyed income gains in their new job relative to their previous job, lower than the 67% recorded among voluntary job switchers.

While the majority of both groups saw higher incomes when they switched jobs, the ministry noted that involuntary job switchers were less likely to surpass earnings made in their old jobs.

Many job switchers moved across industries or occupations. Residents who changed industries typically remained in or moved into industries with above-average productivity, such as wholesale trade and financial and insurance services, while those who changed occupations commonly moved between PMET (professionals, managers, executives and technicians) jobs.

These cross-sector and cross-occupation transitions show how transferable skills and experience can support workers to navigate labour market changes, said MOM.

Job mobility continued to slow across most sectors, including professional services and financial and insurance services, partly reflecting softer hiring and business restructuring.

But the information and communications sector showed an exception, with the share of employed residents who changed jobs edging up from 8.1% in 2025 to 8.7% in 2026. MOM said the increase indicates ongoing workforce reallocation efforts and changing skill needs as firms adapt to technological developments.
